content: Various standardized definitions and systems have been developed to classify the type and severity of injuries. These systems allow for the comparison of medical outcomes among patients with different types and extents of injuries who receive varying treatment and care regimens. Globally, the most widely accepted injury-severity scale is the Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS), which assigns a numerical score to each injury in every body region based on an ordinal scale ranging from 1 to 6. In 1974, the Injury Severity Score (ISS) was introduced as a method to summarize and account for the effects of multiple injuries. The ISS is derived from AIS scores and uses an ordinal scale ranging from 1 to 75. It is calculated by assigning AIS scores to injuries in six body regions (head/neck, face, thorax, abdomen/visceral pelvis, bony pelvis/extremities, and external structures) and then summing the squares of the highest AIS scores in the three most severely injured body regions. Only the most severe injury in each body region is used in the calculation. If an AIS score of 6 is assigned to any body region, the maximal ISS of 75 is automatically assigned. The ISS is an established method for determining the overall severity of injury and correlates with mortality, morbidity, and length of hospital stay. For example, ISS has been used to predict mortality and the risk of post-injury multiple organ failure. In trauma research, ISS is also used to categorize trauma patients into those with severe injuries (ISS > 15) and those with non-severe injuries (ISS ≤ 15). Patients with an ISS of > 16 and age > 55 years have a significantly decreased survival rate. For patients with blunt trauma, survival decreases as ISS scores increase and with advancing age. Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers assess the nature and severity of a patient’s injury, provide treatment, and determine the most appropriate destination facility. Determining the most suitable facility for a given patient’s injury is a complex process that involves the patient’s clinical condition, preferences of the patient and family, state laws or regulations, and the capabilities and capacity of the hospital and EMS system. The accuracy of field triage is defined as the degree of match between the severity of injury and the level of care provided. Sensitivity and specificity are useful indicators of triage accuracy. Triage that successfully transports only patients with high injury severity to a Level I or Level II center maximizes the positive predictive value (PPV) of the process, while triage that transports only patients with low injury severity to lower-level centers maximizes the negative predictive value (NPV). Ideally, all individuals with severe, life-threatening injuries would be transported to a Level I or Level II trauma center, and those with less serious injuries would be transported to lower-level trauma centers or community EDs. However, patient differences, occult injuries, and the complexities of field assessment preclude perfect accuracy in triage decisions. Inaccurate triage resulting in a patient requiring higher-level care not being transported to a Level I or Level II trauma center is termed undertriage. This can result in the patient not receiving the specialized trauma care required. Conversely, overtriage occurs when a patient who does not require care at a higher-level trauma center is transported to such a center, unnecessarily consuming scarce resources. In trauma systems, reductions in undertriage are often accompanied by increases in overtriage, and vice versa. Because the potential harm associated with undertriage (e.g., a patient in need of trauma center care not receiving appropriate care) is high and could result in death or significant morbidity and disability, trauma systems frequently prioritize minimizing undertriage over minimizing overtriage. Target undertriage rates within a trauma system range from 0% to 5% of patients requiring Level I or Level II trauma-center care, depending on the criteria used to determine the undertriage rate. Target overtriage rates vary, with an approximate range of 25% to 50%. As field triage evolves based on new research findings, overtriage rates might be reduced while maintaining low undertriage rates. Field triage experience has confirmed the importance of making correct destination decisions. Studies evaluating the effect of trauma-center care on mortality in moderately to severely injured patients have shown that one-year mortality is lower among severely injured patients treated at Level I trauma centers compared to those treated at large non-trauma-center hospitals. Those treated at Level I trauma centers also have lower in-hospital mortality, fewer deaths at 30 days post-injury, and fewer deaths at 90 days post-injury. Since 1993, crowding in EDs has increased significantly due to reductions in the number of hospitals with EDs, regionalization of surgical care, increases in non-emergency patient visits to EDs, EMS diversions, and personnel shortages.g., on-call coverage and physician commitment), further complicate the situation. For example, in 2001, five public trauma centers in Texas reported a mean operating loss of $18.6 million. The initial cost to establish a trauma center, including verification processes, staffing, on-call coverage, outreach, and prevention, is substantial, with the median annual fixed cost for trauma-center readiness estimated at $2.7 million. The cost of injury in the United States is also significant, exceeding $400 billion in 2000.
